code.title: GitOps reconcile loop: create, patch, prune
code.python:
# Toy GitOps reconcile loop: compare desired (Git) with live (cluster).
desired = ["Deployment/web|replicas|3", "Deployment/web|image|web:1.4", "Service/web|port|80"]
live = ["Deployment/web|replicas|5", "Deployment/web|image|web:1.4",
        "Deployment/web|uid|abc", "Job/debug|image|busybox"]

def reconcile(desired, live):
    want = [d.split("|") for d in desired]
    have = [l.split("|") for l in live]
    have_names = {h[0] for h in have}
    want_names = {w[0] for w in want}
    actions, created = [], set()
    for name, field, value in want:          # only fields Git declares are compared
        if name not in have_names:
            if name not in created:
                created.add(name)
                actions.append("create " + name)
            continue
        for h in have:
            if h[0] == name and h[1] == field and h[2] != value:
                actions.append("patch %s.%s %s -> %s" % (name, field, h[2], value))
    for name in sorted(have_names - want_names):   # in cluster, not in Git: prune
        actions.append("delete " + name)
    return actions

print("desired:", desired)
print("live:", live)
for a in reconcile(desired, live):
    print(a)
# Time O(D*L) here for clarity; with maps it is O(D+L). Space O(D+L).

followUps: CI still needs two things: write access to the config repository and push access to the image registry. It does not need a kubeconfig. Both can be narrow: a deploy key or fine-grained token limited to one repo (and ideally one folder via branch rules), and a registry token that can only push. If someone steals them they can propose a bad change, which review and branch protection catch, but they cannot reach into the cluster directly. The cluster-side agent holds the cluster credentials, and it only needs read access to the repo.

Anything that is data or is decided at runtime cannot live in Git. Examples: database contents and PVC data (use backups), certificates issued at runtime (cert-manager creates the Secret; Git holds only the Certificate request), and autoscaled replica counts (an HPA changes replicas all day). GitOps manages the shape of the system, not its contents. For these fields, drop them from Git or tell the controller to ignore them, for example with ignoreDifferences.

Argo CD runs a health check per resource kind. For a CRD it has no idea what "working" means, so it either uses a check that ships with Argo CD for well-known CRDs (cert-manager Certificate, Rollout) or a Lua script you add in argocd-cm under resource.customizations.health.<group>_<Kind>. The script reads the object's status.conditions and returns Healthy, Progressing or Degraded with a message. Without any check, an unknown CRD is simply reported as Healthy, even if it is broken.

A paused Rollout is not finished and not failed: it is waiting for a person or a timer. Argo CD's health check for Rollouts maps the paused state to Suspended, so you see that the release is stopped on purpose. Example: a canary at 25 percent with a manual pause step shows Suspended until you run kubectl argo rollouts promote. The app's health is the worst of its resources, so the whole Application shows Suspended too.

Because with auto-sync on, the rollback would be undone within minutes. argocd app rollback re-applies an older revision to the cluster but leaves Git alone, so Git HEAD still says the new version and auto-sync would sync straight back. The CLI therefore refuses. The GitOps way is git revert of the bad commit and a push: the fix is reviewed, recorded in history, and applied by the normal loop. If you must roll back by hand in an emergency, disable auto-sync first and write down that you did.

ApplyOutOfSyncOnly=true tells Argo CD to apply only the objects that are actually out of sync instead of every object in the app. In a big app with, say, 800 resources where one ConfigMap changed, a normal sync sends 800 apply calls; with this option it sends 1. That saves time and API load. The trade-off is that a hook or wave still runs normally, and anything not detected as out of sync is not touched, so it will not repair things the diff cannot see.

code.title: Sync order: phase, then wave, then kind
code.python:
# Order a sync: phase, then wave, then kind order, then name.
PHASES = ["PreSync", "Sync", "PostSync"]
KINDS = ["Namespace", "ConfigMap", "Service", "Deployment", "Job"]
items = ["Deployment/web Sync 0", "Job/smoke PostSync 0", "Job/migrate PreSync 0",
         "Service/web Sync 0", "Namespace/shop Sync -1", "ConfigMap/cfg Sync 0"]

def key(item):
    ref, phase, wave = item.split()
    kind, name = ref.split("/")
    return (PHASES.index(phase), int(wave), KINDS.index(kind), name)  # int(): -1 < 0 < 10

print("input:", items)
for item in sorted(items, key=key):
    ref, phase, wave = item.split()
    print("%s %s: %s" % (phase, wave, ref))
# Time O(n log n), space O(n).

followUps: Argo CD translates them: pre-install and pre-upgrade hooks become PreSync, post-install and post-upgrade become PostSync. This works because Argo CD renders the chart with helm template and never creates a real Helm release, so helm list shows nothing. Hooks such as pre-delete or test have no good equivalent and need care. Helm hook weights are not the same as sync waves, so check the order in the rendered output before trusting it.

Because during a rolling update the old Pods keep running against the already migrated database. If the migration drops or renames a column the old code uses, those Pods start failing while the new ones come up. Use expand and contract: first add the new column (old code ignores it), deploy the new code, and only in a later release remove the old column. Example: to rename name to full_name, add full_name, copy data, switch the code, and drop name weeks later. It also makes rollback safe.

Do not take the project from anything a team can edit freely. Hard-code project in the ApplicationSet template, for example project: team-payments, or derive it from something the platform controls, such as the folder path. Then protect that ApplicationSet with CODEOWNERS and with an AppProject that limits which ApplicationSets and namespaces a team may use. If the template read the project from a file the team owns, a team could write project: default and escape its limits.

RollingSync is an alpha ApplicationSet strategy that updates the generated Applications in ordered steps instead of all at once. You label the Applications (for example env=dev, then env=prod) and define steps with a maxUpdate, such as 25 percent at a time. Argo CD waits for each step to be healthy before starting the next. It gives you progressive delivery across many clusters. Because it is not on by default it must be enabled explicitly and its behaviour can change between versions.

Not natively. Argo CD's UI shows Applications, not Flux Kustomization or HelmRelease objects, so Flux-managed workloads appear only as plain Kubernetes resources, if at all. Flux has its own UI options, such as Weave GitOps or the Capacitor dashboard, and its CLI (flux get all). Teams that run both usually give each tool its own layer, for example Flux for cluster add-ons and Argo CD for team apps, and accept two views.

Flux has it built in: the image-reflector and image-automation controllers scan a registry for new tags, then commit the new tag to Git. Argo CD does this with a separate project, Argo CD Image Updater, which watches the registry and either writes back to Git or sets parameters. Both approaches still need a rule that picks versions (for example semver 1.x). Neither should write straight to production without a review gate.

Render both environments in CI and post the difference as a PR comment. A change to a base file can silently change prod; the YAML diff of the overlay alone does not show that. Example: run kustomize build envs/dev and kustomize build envs/prod on the PR branch and on main, then diff the outputs. Tools such as argocd app diff --local, flux diff or kubectl diff do the same against a live cluster. Reviewers then see "prod gets 2 more replicas and a new env var", not just a one-line edit.

In a monorepo every commit would make Argo CD re-render every app. Two fixes: the annotation argocd.argoproj.io/manifest-generate-paths tells Argo CD which folders affect an app, so a commit that touches only apps/b does not re-render app A. And Git webhooks make changes arrive in seconds so you can poll less often. Also add repo-server replicas and caching, keep Helm charts small, and shard the application controller if one controller watches too many objects.

Because nobody reviews or gates it. An image updater that writes to prod ships every new tag the moment it appears, so a broken build goes live with no human check and no proof that it ran well in staging. Prod should move by a promotion pull request that is allowed only after the previous environment is healthy, analysis passed and some soak time (say 2 hours) elapsed. The updater is fine for dev, where speed matters more than control.

Separate what each writer touches and make writes safe to retry. Give CI and the bot different paths (one writes envs/dev/image.yaml, another a different file). Prefer PR-based write-back so conflicts show up as PRs instead of failed pushes. Make commits idempotent: if the tag is already set, do nothing. And on a rejected push, fetch, rebase and retry a few times with a short delay rather than force-pushing, which would erase the other writer's commit.

First rotate the secret, because it is already compromised: anyone who cloned the repo or any fork has it, and removing it later does not undo that. Second, clean the history if policy requires it (git filter-repo), knowing that clones and caches may keep it. Third, add secret scanning in CI and a pre-commit hook, and move the secret to Sealed Secrets, SOPS or External Secrets so it does not happen again.

Not automatically: Kubernetes updates a mounted Secret file after a short delay, but environment variables are fixed when the container starts. Two common fixes: use a tool such as Reloader, which watches the Secret and restarts the Deployment when it changes, or make the app re-read the mounted file periodically. Example: with env vars, a rotated database password needs a rolling restart; with a mounted file and a reloading app there is no restart at all.

code.title: Canary rollout with a metric gate
code.python:
# Model of a canary rollout: raise the weight step by step, check the error rate.
steps = [5, 25, 50, 100]                 # percent of traffic to the new version
# error rate seen at each step; None means the metrics query returned no data
error_rates = [0.004, 0.006, 0.031, 0.002]
MAX_ERROR = 0.01                         # successCondition: result < 1 percent
FAILURE_LIMIT = 0                        # failures tolerated before abort

def run(error_rates):
    failures = 0
    for weight, rate in zip(steps, error_rates):
        if rate is None:
            print("weight %3d%%: no data -> Inconclusive, pause for a human" % weight)
            return "Paused"
        ok = rate < MAX_ERROR
        print("weight %3d%%: error rate %.1f%% -> %s" % (weight, rate * 100, "pass" if ok else "FAIL"))
        if not ok:
            failures += 1
            if failures > FAILURE_LIMIT:
                print("abort: traffic back to stable (Git still holds the bad version)")
                return "Aborted"
    return "Promoted"

print("steps:", steps)
print("result:", run(error_rates))
print("result:", run([0.004, None, 0.0, 0.0]))
print("result:", run([0.004, 0.006, 0.002, 0.002]))
# Time O(steps), space O(1).

followUps: Use blue-green: bring up the new version beside the old one with no user traffic, test it, then switch traffic all at once (and switch back if needed). Canary needs both versions to serve real requests at the same time. Even with blue-green, the database must work with both versions during the switch, so keep schema changes expand then contract. Cost: you briefly run double the Pods, for example 20 instead of 10.

Run the same query for the canary and for the stable version and compare them, instead of using a fixed number. Example condition: canary error rate divided by stable error rate must be below 1.5. This works when the whole system is having a bad day (both rates are high, the ratio is still 1) where a fixed threshold of 1 percent would fail the canary wrongly. Guard against divide by zero and tiny samples, and still require a minimum request count.

code.title: Why OutOfSync: ignore rules and normalising
code.python:
# Why an app is OutOfSync after every sync, and how an ignore rule fixes it.
git = {"replicas": "3", "image": "web:1.4", "cpu": "1"}
# live: the HPA changed replicas, and the API server wrote the CPU as "1000m"
live = {"replicas": "7", "image": "web:1.4", "cpu": "1000m", "uid": "abc"}

def normalise(key, value):
    if key == "cpu" and value.endswith("m"):       # 1000m is the same as 1
        return str(int(value[:-1]) // 1000)
    return value

def diff(git, live, ignore=()):
    out = []
    for key, want in git.items():                   # live-only keys (uid) are skipped
        if key in ignore:
            continue
        have = normalise(key, live.get(key, "<none>"))
        if have != want:
            out.append("%s: %s -> %s" % (key, have, want))
    return out

print("git:", git)
print("live:", live)
print("diff after normalising cpu:", diff(git, {k: v for k, v in live.items()}, ignore=()))
print("raw string compare of cpu would also differ:", git["cpu"] != live["cpu"])
print("ignore replicas (HPA owns it):", diff(git, live, ignore=("replicas",)))
print("ignore everything would hide real drift:", diff(git, live, ignore=("replicas", "image", "cpu")))
# Time O(keys), space O(keys).

followUps: Because it can hide real drift. An ignore rule on a whole section, for example /spec, means nobody is told when someone changes the image or the security context by hand. Keep rules narrow: one field, one kind (for example /spec/replicas on Deployments owned by an HPA), with a comment saying who owns it. Review ignore rules in PRs like code, and prefer removing the field from Git or using server-side diff first.

With ServerSideDiff=true Argo CD asks the API server to run the apply as a dry run and compares that result with live, instead of comparing raw YAML. The server has already added defaults and run mutating webhooks, so those fields no longer appear as differences. Example: Git omits imagePullPolicy, live has IfNotPresent; a plain diff may flag it, the server-side diff does not. The cost is an extra API call per resource.

Nothing happens to the apps that are already running: Argo CD is a control loop, not part of the data path. Pods keep serving, Services keep routing. What pauses is deployments, drift correction and status: new commits are not applied, self-heal does not run, and the UI is gone. When Argo CD returns it reconciles to the latest Git state. So an outage of the tool is a deploy freeze, not a production outage, which is why you still need a break-glass path for urgent fixes.

Treat it like any other app: change it through Git. Pin the version in the config repo, read the release notes (for example the 2.x to 3.x upgrade notes), then upgrade a staging instance first and watch sync results for a day. Production comes next, one region or one instance at a time, with the previous version one revert away. Back up the Application and AppProject objects and settings first. Never upgrade every control plane in one step.

Because a UI rollback changes only the cluster, while Git still says the bad version. Auto-sync would put the bad version back, and anyone reading Git would think prod runs it. A git revert of the promotion commit keeps Git as the truth, goes through the same pipeline, leaves a record in history, and the same loop applies it everywhere that commit was promoted. Example: revert commit a1b2c3, push, and Argo CD rolls prod back within a minute with a webhook.

Make the pause visible and temporary. Open a ticket when you suspend, and set an alert on suspended Kustomizations (Flux metrics) or on Applications with sync disabled for more than, say, 1 hour. Add a reminder in the incident checklist: "resume reconciliation" is a closing step, and the postmortem checks it. Some teams also add an annotation with the owner and a time and have a job that flags stale ones. Without this, a forgotten suspend silently turns GitOps off.
